comments.author: @kate2create738
comments.text:
One a side note to put in is how different the empires had prioritized the colonies that led each country in the American hemisphere to turn out so differently. The Spanish clearly used colonialism as a way to extract, finding that much silver really enabled this. The English tried that but they landed in a region where no gold or silver was in site. A big key take away is the Anglo culture from my observation has an ability to adapt, I give credit to the UK being an island nation where their neighbor France is always in a rocky relationship and the fighting of the kingdoms among themselves, had developed a culture to adapt. So the lower regions of the colonies eventually adapted to lucrative commodities to certain products that the UK had no way in obtaining. The northern colonies were developed in fear of persecution because of how turbulent the European religious setting was, they decided to risk it all in the New World with little preparation was worth it than to be on their toes if new management comes and declares a new way to practice their beliefs and life. Keep in mind both regions actually really struggled to survive, Jamestown went into starvation because the colony was intended for extracting resources and no concept of building civilization they didn’t know how to forage their own food, at times it went into cannibalism. 💀 The Plymouth colonies were severely unprepared because of how quickly they had to leave, 50% of the voyage was lost that winter. They worked hard to try to cohabit with the natives, to learn of the land, to try to not get too caught up their tribalistic politics of the natives. Because it was set up as a colony to start a new society, the Plymouth colony made efforts to think more in the mindset of what they were able to accomplish to survive winter but also to think long term. 


To add one other important detail, the English colonies were adamant in insisting everyone was educated in some form, not only to have a skill to help build a community, but that the people were critical thinkers. Learned recently that apparently by the time the 13 colonies were in the 1700’s, it was actually the most educated concentrated region in the world of that time. Plymouth and the rest of the colony first started off teaching children to read by reading the Bible. As the colonies grew, the more sophisticated the academics became that it was common for women to partake in literature and philosophy while men were knowledgeable in Ancient Greek and Roman way of life. You can really tell how much the founding fathers of the US had deep admiration and respect towards Ancient Roman and the Greeks, we have an architecture period of our early days as a new country called the Federation period and the Revival Federation a few generations later to highlight Ancient Roman and Greek inspiration. 

To read is very important, it shares knowledge and information, it played a big part in connecting the 13 colonies despite how different they were. It brought inspiration and helped formed new ideas to test out. The Spanish I don’t think prioritized this, mostly in the higher status of the colonies but in general it wasn’t important to spread to everyone.
